hints: Focus on what type of reaction happens when an alkene meets Br2 or HBr in the dark, electrophilic addition across the double bond.
Remember propene is unsymmetrical, so addition of HBr can put H on either carbon to give both 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane.
Ask yourself where the two Br atoms must end up if you add Br-Br across C=C in one step, and whether both can land on the same carbon.
walkthrough:
**Identify the conditions**

Great start, notice the key phrase: in the dark. That tells us there is no UV light, so no free radical substitution. Only electrophilic addition to the C=C bond can happen.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{E-E} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(E)}-\text{CH}_2\text{(E)}$$

**Add HBr to propene**

Propene is unsymmetrical, so the H can add to either end of the double bond. This gives two possible monobromo products.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3 \text{ (major, Markovnikov)} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br (minor)}$$

**Add Br2 to propene**

Bromine adds across the double bond with one Br on each carbon. There is only one way to do this.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$$

**Spot the impossible product**

Addition always puts one atom on each carbon of the original double bond. So 1,2-dibromopropane forms easily, but 1,1-dibromopropane with both Br atoms on carbon 1 cannot form by addition.

options.A: 1-bromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, is present as the minor anti-Markovnikov product of HBr addition. The less stable primary carbocation forms in very small quantity, but the question says to include very small quantities.
options.B: 2-bromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$, is present as the major Markovnikov product of HBr addition. H adds to C1 to give the more stable secondary carbocation, then $\text{Br}^-$ attacks C2.
options.C: 1,1-dibromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBr}_2$, will not be present. Electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2$ must place one Br on each carbon of the double bond to give the 1,2-isomer. Putting both Br atoms on the same carbon cannot happen by this mechanism in the dark.
options.D: 1,2-dibromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$, is present as the normal electrophilic addition product of $\text{Br}_2$ to propene. One Br adds to C1 and the other to C2.
